programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: Clinton Kelly and Stacy London break down the iconic costumes in "When Harry Met Sally," designed by Gloria Gresham. The hosts trace fashion evolution across the film's 12-year timeline, from 1977 collegiate casual wear through early-80s yuppie aesthetics to late-80s power dressing and evening wear. They discuss standout pieces including Sally's navy knee-highs with shorts, the infamous oversized plaid sweater from the orgasm scene, off-shoulder dresses, and bridesmaid gowns. The analysis balances appreciation for authentic period styling with candid critiques of questionable fit and silhouette choices, ultimately celebrating how the costumes authentically capture the era without overshadowing the film's acclaimed dialogue.

programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: Clinton Kelly and Stacy London break down the costume design of Steel Magnolias, the 1989 Herbert Ross-directed classic that defined 80s Southern fashion. Examining 12 key looks worn by the ensemble cast—including Dolly Parton, Julia Roberts, Sally Field, Olympia Dukakis, and Shirley MacLaine—the hosts praise costume designer Julie Weiss's work while debating which outfits have aged well. They celebrate the film's mastery of pastels, accessories, and hair, though they critique questionable choices like an unflattering bridesmaid dress and one of Julia Roberts's worst wigs. The episode culminates in a discussion of the Easter scene's spring renewal and final ratings.

programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: Clinton Kelly and Stacy London explore the costume design and fashion choices in Dirty Dancing, the 1987 film set in 1963. They discuss how the opening scenes use wardrobe to establish character contrasts between Baby and her sister, analyze the significance of the "dirty dancing" club scene, and examine Baby's transformation through costume as she becomes involved with dance instructor Johnny. The hosts debate period authenticity, particularly noting anachronistic elements like Penny's disco-influenced styling, and praise how costume design communicates character development and social themes throughout the film.

programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: Clinton Kelly and Stacy London welcome special guest Carla Hall to examine the costume design of the 1954 musical film Carmen Jones, based on Bizet's opera. The trio analyzes 10 key looks from the film, exploring Dorothy Dandridge's evolution from the seductive factory worker in a red wrap skirt to her glamorous final appearance in a sequined gown. They discuss costume choices that reflect character development, debate whether 1954 silhouettes were used instead of period-appropriate 1940s styles, and examine how accessories either enhance or overwhelm the overall aesthetic. The conversation touches on representation, beauty standards of the era, and what each character's wardrobe reveals about her personality and arc.

programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: Clinton Kelly and Stacy London dissect the intentional costume choices in The Housemaid, directed by Paul Feig and designed by Renée Ehrlich Kalfus. Through eight awards and superlatives, they explore how the film's palette of cashmere sweaters, scarves, and neutral tones reflects the psychological manipulation at the story's core. From the protagonist's revealing first-day outfit to the terrifying mother-in-law's black-and-white aesthetic, each costume detail reinforces character dynamics. The hosts discuss how fabric choices, color progression, and styling decisions—from vibrant pre-marriage fuchsia to subdued whites and beiges—illustrate the protagonist's loss of agency. They highlight standout looks including a peplum top, funeral attire with snowflake buttons, and an endless supply of luxury cashmere pieces.

programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: Clinton Kelly and Stacy London dive into the costumes of the 1986 film Pretty in Pink, directed by Howard Deutch with costume design by Marilyn Vance. The episode celebrates how the movie uses vintage and secondhand clothing as a love letter to sustainable fashion, analyzing 12 iconic looks from characters including Andie (Molly Ringwald), Duckie (Jon Cryer), Blane (Andrew McCarthy), and Iona (Annie Potts). The hosts discuss how layering, pattern-mixing, and thrifted pieces create personal style that stands out from mainstream 1980s fashion, while also addressing the film's controversial ending and the infamous final prom dress that nearly every production member disliked.

programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: Hosts Clinton Kelly and Stacy London examine the costume design of Ang Lee's The Ice Storm, a 1997 film set in 1973 suburban Connecticut during Thanksgiving. Costume designer Carol Oditz dresses the cast in period-accurate polyester, capes, palazzo pants, and crocheted tunics as the characters navigate infidelity and a notorious key party. The hosts break down seven standout looks, from Kevin Kline's oversized collar and dickey to Sigourney Weaver's strategic halter top and beaded necklace at the pivotal party scene. They discuss the film's maximalist 70s aesthetic, the significance of color symbolism, and which characters actually understood the assignment of getting laid.

programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: Clinton Kelly and Stacy London analyze St. Elmo's Fire, the 1985 ensemble film that inspired a generation. The hosts count down their top five favorite fashion looks from the movie, with three featuring Demi Moore's glamorous character Jules in bold '80s styles including rhinestone details, fur stoles, and statement jewelry. They also identify three of the film's cringiest moments, from Rob Lowe's saxophone scene to the infamous scuba suit sequence.

programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: In this episode of "Why'd They Wear That?," hosts Clinton Kelly and Stacy London explore the visual style of Tony Scott's 1983 cult classic "The Hunger," featuring Catherine Deneuve and David Bowie as centuries-old vampires. The hosts examine nine distinct fashion moments from the film, analyzing how costume designer Milena Canonero masterfully blends 1940s silhouettes with 1980s sensibilities. They discuss iconic pieces including leather catsuits, garrison caps, oversized blazers, trenches, and statement accessories like an ornate salamander brooch. The conversation highlights how the costumes reveal character, wealth, and sophistication, while exploring the film's enduring influence on fashion and the practical challenges of recreating these looks today.

programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: Clinton Kelly and Stacy London dive into the wardrobes of Grease's secondary characters, exploring the film's iconic 1950s-inspired costumes. They discuss Stockard Channing's chic black shirt dress as Rizzo, Frenchie's memorable pink hair sequence, the contrast between good girl Patty Simcox and bad girl Cha Cha DiGregorio, and standout prom looks including velvet green dresses and sequined designs. The hosts also reflect on the film's casting of actors in their 30s as high schoolers and debate the merits of Sandy's transformation into "bad Sandy" by film's end, while appreciating costume designer Albert Wolsky's bold color and pattern choices throughout.

programme.title: Why'd They Wear That?
programme.desc: Clinton Kelly and Stacy London dive into six of cinema and television's most distractingly impractical outfits that steal focus from the story. The hosts discuss Milla Jovovich's enigmatic bandage-like ensemble in The Fifth Element designed by Jean Paul Gaultier, Bryce Dallas Howard's high heels while running from a dinosaur in Jurassic World, Blake Lively's haute couture floristry in It Ends with Us, Kerry Washington's signature white coat in Scandal that would never survive a day in Washington D.C., and Kaitlin Olson's impractically short miniskirt at crime scenes in High Potential. Throughout the episode, they explore why costume designers and actors make questionable practical choices and how these wardrobe decisions become more distracting than the actual plot.

programme.title: Simply Symons
programme.desc: In the debut episode of Simply Symons, Michael Symon welcomes viewers into his Venice, California front yard alongside his wife Liz Symon and their friend Olivia Annacone Cisic for an unfiltered, laid-back cookout. Celebrating Cinco de Mayo, Michael prepares simple yet flavorful black cod fish tacos on a plancha, walking through his approach to seasoning, cooking fish by sight, and building a bright, crunchy slaw with cabbage, citrus, and charred poblanos. The conversation flows easily as the trio shares cooking tips, debates ingredients like corn versus flour tortillas, and jokes about knife sharpening habits, cilantro preferences, and home cooking realities. Liz complements the meal with a refreshing jalapeño margarita, balancing heat with fresh lime juice, simple syrup, and a hint of orange liqueur, while adding her own creative twist with lemon and bitters. Throughout the episode, the group emphasizes flexibility in cooking—encouraging viewers to adjust flavors, garnishes, and spice levels to their own tastes. Lighthearted banter continues as they assemble tacos, discuss plating ideas, and highlight optional additions like crema and avocado. The episode wraps with a taste test, enthusiastic reactions to both the tacos and cocktail, and a reminder that great food doesn’t have to be complicated—just fresh, simple, and made with joy.

programme.title: Simply Symons
programme.desc: Michael Symon, Liz Symon, and Olivia Annacone Cisic tackle a brunch-inspired twist on eggs Benedict by swapping traditional Canadian bacon for crispy pastrami and pairing it with a mustard-spiked hollandaise sauce. Michael walks through a foolproof blender hollandaise method while explaining the science behind emulsifying butter and keeping the sauce warm, making the intimidating brunch staple feel approachable for home cooks. As the family cooks together, the conversation bounces between Olivia’s skepticism about poached eggs, Liz’s love of runny yolks, and memories of iconic pastrami spots like Langer’s and Katz’s. The group also debates poaching techniques, from classic whirlpool methods to muffin tin hacks for feeding a crowd. Humor carries the episode throughout as Michael teases Olivia’s picky eating habits and the family jokes about “buttering muffins” and hollandaise disasters. Liz complements the rich brunch dish with a citrus-forward mimosa made from blood oranges, sumo oranges, lemon juice, and frozen strawberries used as flavorful ice cubes. Once plated, the pastrami Benedict wins Olivia over completely, with the crispy pastrami and tangy mustard hollandaise becoming the standout combination. The episode wraps with the family enjoying brunch cocktails, discussing make-ahead egg tips, and Michael reminding viewers that restaurant-quality brunch can come together quickly and simply at home.

programme.title: Simply Symons
programme.desc: Michael Symon kicks off a new era of Simply Symons from Venice, California, joined by Liz Symon and Olivia “Liv” Annacone Cisic for a laid-back backyard cookout centered around the ultimate burger debate: smash burgers versus classic pub burgers. Michael walks through the techniques behind each style, from selecting the ideal fat ratio for ground beef to achieving the perfect crust on a hot grill and cast iron griddle. Along the way, the trio shares stories about old Symon’s Dinners episodes, Liv’s transition into motherhood, and the realities of filming outdoors with planes overhead, lawn equipment buzzing nearby, and neighborhood life unfolding around them. As Michael builds both burgers with grilled onions, pickles, secret sauce, and different cheeses, the conversation turns into a humorous discussion about condiments, cooking preferences, smash burger myths, and burger nostalgia. Liz keeps the energy going with playful jabs at Michael while also preparing his favorite cocktail, the bourbon-based Paper Plane, complete with Aperol, Amaro, and fresh lemon juice. The episode wraps with a tasting session comparing both burgers side-by-side, with everyone weighing in on which version wins the battle. Between the casual banter, cooking tips, and family-style atmosphere, the episode delivers an easygoing and highly approachable backyard burger feast.

programme.title: Simply Symons
programme.desc: In this Memorial Day-themed episode of Simply Symons, Michael Symon cooks outdoors with his wife Liz and co-host Olivia Annacone Cisic, preparing grilled shrimp skewers with a honey-soy-orange glaze, a pineapple salsa, and a coconut rice pilaf, while Liz mixes up a frothy pineapple daiquiri with an egg-white twist. The episode opens with playful banter about Olivia's discovery of gray hairs at 33, her upcoming bachelorette party plans, and Michael's gentle ribbing of the trio's early-dinner, early-bedtime lifestyle. Michael walks through his Memorial Day menu, highlighting a coconut rice made with jasmine rice, coconut milk, and a coconut curry lime bone broth from friend Marco Canora's brand Brodo, plus a bright pineapple salsa built with cilantro, scallion, red pepper, jalapeño, honey, and a dashi soy sauce sourced from Santa Monica's McCall's butcher. A lively debate breaks out over rice ratios and rinsing technique, with Liz advocating for a 1:1¾ ratio while Michael sticks to his two-to-one method, and Olivia sharing that she recently cooked jasmine rice for her unwell dog Zeke. Throughout the cooking session, mishaps and humor keep things lively — limes refuse to juice, Liz nearly topples the dashi bottle, and Michael accidentally steps on their dog Min. Discussions range from shrimp varieties and sizing (the U-number system), to the fruity heat of jalapeños and habaneros, to favorite hot sauces including Crystal and the Florida datil-pepper-based Zabs. Liz's honest palate becomes a recurring theme, with Michael crediting her direct, critical feedback as a key ingredient in his culinary success over the years. Liz dry-shakes her egg-white pineapple daiquiri before adding ice for a frothy finish, then adjusts the balance mid-tasting by swirling in extra pineapple juice. The shrimp grill up with beautiful caramelization from the honey glaze, and the coconut rice is finished simply with cilantro and cracked black pepper. During the final tasting, Olivia — a self-described texture-averse pasta lover — bravely tries the shrimp, endorsing the flavors while admitting she prefers the coconut rice. Michael closes the episode wishing viewers a happy Memorial Day and reminding them to keep things simple and delicious.

programme.title: The Tuskegee Airmen: Return to Ramitelli
programme.desc: THE TUSKEGEE AIRMEN: RETURN TO RAMITELLI tells the story of a legendary United States Air Force squadron comprised entirely of Black soldiers. Until 1941, Black soldiers in the U.S. military were considered unfit for service and were limited to positions as cooks and stewards. However, that all changed when the United States Department of War authorized the creation of an all-Black fighter unit known as the Tuskegee Airmen. The squadrons record of success would heavily contribute to the desegregation of the U.S. military only seven years after its formation.In this documentary, veteran Tuskegee Airmen return to visit the site of their operations in Ramitelli Italy. We experience their legacy through World War II-era footage, animated reenactments, and interviews with Tuskegee veterans and historians.

programme.title: Survivors of Malmedy: December 1944
programme.desc: SURVIVORS OF MALMEDY: DECEMBER 1944 tells the story of the World War II massacre of 84 American soldiers in Belgium during the opening days of the famous Battle of the Bulge.On December 17, 1944, after a short battle, more than 130 American GIs were taken prisoner just outside the Belgian town of Malmedy and herded into a field by an infamous German SS division led by one of the Nazi's most brutal commanders. The unarmed American prisoners were gunned down. Those still alive after the initial shooting in the brutal cold were killed by SS soldiers ordered into the field to execute any Americans still breathing. Some American soldiers played dead. Some ran. Some escaped to nearby houses. In the end, more than 50 Americans did escape the infamous Malmedy Massacre. Today, just a handful of soldiers remain.Weaving interviews with the few remaining survivors of the massacre with archival footage, and drone video shot in the Malmedy area and in the field where the infamous event occurred, the emotional and powerful SURVIVORS OF MALMEDY chronicles what became known as the largest single mass murder of American troops in World War II.
